strengths: The task—continuing an arbitrarily long video while preserving the scene and following a target camera path—is important and clearly motivated. The dual temporal/static-spatial conditioning formulation is intuitive. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/ded12cb8d81444878ba6456fcf2d4552/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The integration of dynamic SLAM, motion-based masking, tracking, segmentation, and projected point-cloud prompts forms a coherent practical pipeline. Reusing CogVideoX with limited architectural modification is appealing.

Results against DFoT are substantial on the proposed revisit evaluation: for example, RealEstate10K MEt3R improves from 0.1812 to 0.0408 and PSNR from 18.30 to 20.89. Experiments cover 1,000 static and 1,000 dynamic videos and report several complementary metrics.

The paper is generally clear and visually polished, with useful system diagrams and qualitative comparisons. Training hardware, duration, optimizer, window size, and number of retrieved views are reported.
weaknesses: The main comparisons are not adequately controlled. Camera-control and video-quality baselines receive a single image or only text, whereas the proposed method receives nine recent frames plus target-aligned projections derived from the full input. Differences in backbone, training data, and conditioning information make the claimed superiority in Tables 2–3 difficult to attribute to the proposed technique.

The spatial-consistency evaluation compares against only DFoT. Geometry-grounded alternatives such as Gen3C, ReCamMaster, and TrajectoryCrafter are dismissed as addressing dynamic novel-view synthesis, yet the paper's evaluation deliberately revisits observed viewpoints and therefore substantially overlaps their setting. Adapted versions and simpler warp/inpainting baselines are needed.

The ablation study is insufficient to establish the contribution of the proposed design. It does not remove temporal or spatial conditioning, compare static memory with raw retrieved frames, isolate the three masking stages, compare alternative masks, or test robustness to erroneous SLAM poses and masks. The single no-mask result cannot validate the complete masking pipeline.

The central arbitrary-length and computational-efficiency claims are unsupported. There is no input-length sweep, memory/runtime analysis, maximum tested duration, or comparison of end-to-end preprocessing cost. MegaSAM, optical flow, CoTracker, and SAM2 must process the context, so efficient generation alone does not establish an efficient overall system.

Evaluation on dynamic videos masks dynamic regions when measuring scene consistency, while generic VBench metrics do not test whether moving objects continue coherently from their recent states. Thus, the claim that dynamic content evolves naturally—the main motivation for static-only memory—is not directly validated.

MegaSAM is used both to construct conditioning geometry and to recover camera trajectories for evaluation, creating possible estimator-specific bias. Results lack confidence intervals or statistical tests; notably, the camera-control improvement over DFoT is small for rotation error. Independent pose estimators and ground-truth-pose evaluations would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is limited: the numbers and selection criteria for training clips, output length and resolution, masking threshold, chosen optical-flow implementation, field-of-view overlap computation, projection/visibility handling, prompt protocol, and detailed evaluation settings are missing. No code, model, or data-processing release is stated.

The technical novelty is primarily a composition of existing pretrained components, so unusually rigorous controlled evaluation is needed. In its current form, the incomplete and potentially unfair comparisons leave the paper below the acceptance bar. The manuscript also lacks a limitations or broader-impact discussion despite foreseeable misuse and dataset-bias concerns for realistic video generation.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: continuing a dynamic video under a specified camera trajectory while preserving scene information observed much earlier in the input. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/eeaeceed29ef471086982312b30c8ec8/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The separation of recent-frame temporal conditioning from static, viewpoint-aligned spatial conditioning is intuitive and practically relevant.
Constructing a static-only point cloud using motion detection, tracking, and segmentation is a sensible way to prevent obsolete dynamic objects from being copied into future frames.
The reported results are consistently favorable across reconstruction, camera-pose, FVD, and VBench++ metrics, and the qualitative figures illustrate the intended behavior clearly.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not provide sufficiently fair or comprehensive comparisons. Camera-control baselines receive only a single image or text while the proposed method receives nine recent frames plus geometry aggregated from the full context. For the central scene-consistency claim, only DFoT is compared, despite closely related geometry-grounded systems such as Gen3C, ReCamMaster, and TrajectoryCrafter.

The central design is inadequately ablated. There is no temporal-only baseline, spatial-only baseline, raw spatial-frame conditioning baseline, or comparison against an unmodified CogVideoX continuation model. The individual stages of the dynamic-mask pipeline are also not evaluated. Consequently, the results do not establish which proposed components are responsible for the gains.

The provided ablations are weak and partly contradict the presentation. Changing the number of retrieved views produces negligible and non-monotonic differences, while removing dynamic masking causes only modest degradation in several metrics. No uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests are reported.

The paper claims arbitrary-length conditioning, long-range consistency, and computational efficiency, but evaluates neither scaling nor genuinely long-horizon recursive generation. Input lengths, output length T, runtime, peak memory, point-cloud growth, and quality as context length or revisit interval increases are not reported.

The evaluation protocol risks circularity: MegaSAM constructs the geometry that guides generation and is also used to recover generated camera poses for camera-control evaluation. Independent pose estimators or direct geometric evaluations are needed. Translation-error normalization and trajectory alignment are also unspecified.

Potential training/evaluation leakage is not resolved. RealEstate10K is used for both training and testing without a stated disjoint split. Moreover, training preprocessing estimates geometry over the entire video, and the described backward-tracking mask aggregates evidence across all frames; it is unclear whether ground-truth future frames influence masks applied to conditioning frames.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript omits essential details including dataset sizes and mixture ratios, exact train/test splits, target length and resolution, frame rate, inference settings, the selected optical-flow model, threshold tau, field-of-view overlap computation, point-cloud fusion and rendering procedures, and handling of holes or SLAM failures.

The method is a composition of existing dynamic SLAM, optical flow, CoTracker, SAM2, point-cloud rendering, and fine-tuning of CogVideoX. The future-generation setting and static filtering are useful, but the technical novelty is limited relative to the strength and breadth of the claims.

There is no human evaluation of identity preservation, motion naturalness, or perceptual scene consistency, and no analysis of important failure cases such as inaccurate SLAM, independently moving cameras or objects, nonrigid backgrounds, lighting changes, large extrapolations, or insufficient static geometry. The paper also omits a limitations and broader-impact discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: camera-controlled continuation that remains consistent with a long input video while allowing dynamic content to evolve.

The central design is compelling and technically intuitive. Combining recent temporal frames with target-view renderings from a static-only 3D scene memory cleanly separates short-term motion continuity from long-range spatial consistency.
The dynamic-masking pipeline—flow residuals, backward point tracking, and SAM2 propagation—is a useful practical contribution for preventing moving objects from becoming ghost geometry.

Experiments cover 1,000 static and 1,000 dynamic videos and evaluate complementary aspects including appearance consistency, multiview geometry, camera accuracy, FVD, and VBench++. The gains over DFoT are substantial, especially on RealEstate10K and MEt3R.
The method makes economical use of a strong pretrained video model: the DiT architecture remains unchanged, and the additional conditions are introduced through the existing conditioning pathway.

The paper is well motivated, clearly organized, and supported by informative qualitative examples. weaknesses: The most important ablations are missing. The paper does not compare the full method against temporal-only conditioning, unmasked 2D spatial retrieval, or spatial conditioning without the proposed 3D memory. Consequently, the reported improvement cannot be cleanly attributed to the central dual-conditioning design.

The scene-consistency comparison includes only DFoT. Relevant geometry-conditioned or video-rendering methods such as Gen3C, ReCamMaster, and TrajectoryCrafter are discussed but not empirically adapted or compared. Even if their original settings differ, stronger adapted baselines would substantially improve the evidence.

Comparisons with camera-control baselines are not fully input-matched: competing methods receive one image or text, whereas the proposed model receives nine frames plus rendered 3D context. These results demonstrate the advantage of the overall task setup but do not isolate a better camera-control mechanism.

The claim of supporting arbitrary-length inputs without significant overhead is insufficiently validated. There is no scaling experiment or report of SLAM preprocessing time, point-cloud memory, rendering cost, or end-to-end latency as input duration grows.

Evaluation of dynamic scenes masks dynamic regions for spatial metrics, while the paper does not directly measure whether foreground motion remains temporally correct or whether removed objects are plausibly regenerated. VBench dynamic degree is too coarse to establish this central claim.

The dynamic-mask heuristic has plausible failure modes—camera-motion or flow errors, nonrigid motion, occlusion, objects entering after the first frame, and imperfect SAM2 masks—but mask accuracy and robustness are not quantitatively evaluated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the numbers and mixture of training samples, resolution, generated length T, flow threshold, viewpoint-overlap computation, projection/hole handling, sampling protocol, and variance or confidence intervals are absent. Code and trained-model availability are also not stated.

The paper lacks a limitations and broader-impact discussion, particularly concerning inherited generative-model biases, privacy and copyright in long-video processing, and misuse for scene-consistent synthetic footage.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem: maintaining long-range scene consistency while controlling the camera and allowing dynamic content to evolve.

The dual conditioning design is intuitive and technically meaningful: recent frames provide temporal continuity, while target-view renderings of a static 3D memory provide spatial guidance without modifying the DiT backbone.

The three-stage dynamic-masking pipeline combining flow residuals, backward point tracking, and SAM2 is well motivated, and the qualitative examples clearly illustrate why removing dynamic geometry matters.

The empirical results are broad and generally favorable, covering spatial consistency, geometric consistency, camera control, video quality, runtime, long-video generation, and multiple component ablations. The large MEt3R improvement over DFoT is particularly promising.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and candid about dependence on SLAM and mask quality. Experiments replacing MegaSAM with DepthAnything v3 also support the claimed modularity.
weaknesses: The central long-range scene-consistency comparison is insufficiently comprehensive: Table 1 compares only against DFoT. Closely related geometry- or memory-based systems such as Gen3C, ReCamMaster, SPMem, WorldMem, and newer multi-frame camera-control methods are discussed but not empirically compared. This makes it difficult to establish state-of-the-art significance.

Several comparisons are not fully controlled. The proposed model is fine-tuned on roughly 50K curated videos and receives substantially richer video and geometry context, whereas many camera-control baselines receive only one image or text. Consequently, the gains in FVD and VBench cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed spatial prompting mechanism. The long-video baselines also use different extension strategies, weakening Table 5's fairness.

The claim of supporting arbitrary-length context is stronger than the evidence. Experiments do not vary input-context length, report performance as context grows, or characterize preprocessing memory and runtime as a function of length. The 180-frame autoregressive examples evaluate a different claim and still exhibit acknowledged error accumulation.

Evaluation on dynamic scenes masks dynamic regions when computing scene-consistency metrics. This validates preservation of the static background but does not substantiate the central assertion that dynamic objects evolve naturally while retaining appropriate identity and motion continuity. VBench aggregates generic quality properties and is not a substitute for targeted dynamic-object evaluation or a human study.

Important protocol and implementation details are underspecified, including the precise tensor construction and alignment of the temporal and spatial conditions, target trajectory generation, train/test separation for the curated data, camera-error alignment and normalization, thresholds used by dynamic masking, sampling settings, and random-seed variability. The paper reports no confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics, and code is only promised.

Some ablation conclusions are overstated. For example, adding SAM2 propagation in Table 6 worsens MEt3R relative to the preceding flow-mask variant, so the results do not uniformly demonstrate that every stage is independently beneficial. The choice n=7 is also only marginally differentiated from smaller values.

The method depends on accurate SLAM, calibration, optical flow, tracking, and segmentation, but robustness is not tested under failed pose estimation, fast or nonrigid motion, severe occlusion, low texture, moving cameras with dominant foreground objects, or inaccurate intrinsics. These are likely practical failure modes for the stated real-world setting.

The submission lacks a meaningful discussion of data licensing, privacy, misuse, and representational risks associated with training on large-scale web video and enabling controllable realistic video generation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: preserving long-range scene identity while allowing dynamic content to evolve under explicit camera control.
The dual temporal/spatial conditioning idea is intuitive, and the use of a static-only 3D memory provides a sensible mechanism for separating persistent geometry from transient motion.
The method makes relatively small changes to the CogVideoX backbone and is modular with respect to the underlying geometry estimator.

Experiments cover several dimensions—scene consistency, camera control, video quality, runtime, and long-video generation—and report sizable gains over the selected baselines. The component, temporal-window, and projected-view ablations are useful.
The qualitative results generally support improved scene preservation, and the paper is organized clearly with helpful pipeline visualizations.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method largely composes dynamic SLAM, optical-flow residuals, CoTracker, SAM2, point-cloud projection, and an existing video diffusion model. The distinction from closely related geometry-memory approaches, especially SPMem, Gen3C, ReCamMaster, and TrajectoryCrafter, is argued verbally but not established through direct experiments.

The central scene-consistency comparison includes only DFoT. Several relevant geometry-conditioned or long-memory systems are omitted, and the comparisons against CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, and AC3D involve different backbones, conditioning information, and training setups. Consequently, the reported video-quality gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed contribution.

The evaluation is unusually favorable to the method: scene consistency is measured primarily on trajectories revisiting observed viewpoints, where projected input geometry directly supplies the answer. There is little evaluation on extrapolative camera paths, poorly covered regions, severe occlusion, or SLAM failure cases.

MegaSAM is involved in constructing the method's representation and in recovering camera poses for camera-control evaluation, creating potential estimator bias. The paper does not provide an independent pose evaluation, human study, or uncertainty analysis.

The claimed support for arbitrary-length context is not convincingly demonstrated. There is no sweep over input length, memory growth, SLAM runtime, or reconstruction degradation. The long-video experiment instead evaluates autoregressive output to only 180 frames and uses loosely matched baseline extensions.

The dynamic-masking pipeline is not evaluated directly against segmentation ground truth. Its ablation is on an unspecified subset and does not test difficult cases such as newly appearing objects, nonrigid motion, reflections, shadows, or objects that are absent from the first frame.

The efficiency claims are overstated. The reported DepthAnything-v3 configuration takes about 5.2 minutes versus 1.6–2.2 minutes for CameraCtrl and MotionCtrl, while the MegaSAM version takes over 9 minutes; this is neither negligible overhead nor clearly comparable latency.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the stated intention to release code. Important details are missing, including the motion threshold, point-sampling rules, data-filtering criteria, trajectory construction, inference settings, and precise metric alignment or units. Results also lack variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

The paper provides no meaningful ethical discussion of generative-video misuse, privacy, dataset licensing, or deepfake risks. Overall, the idea is promising and technically plausible, but the evidence and comparisons fall marginally short of the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem: extending arbitrary-length dynamic videos under user-specified camera trajectories while preserving previously observed scene structure.

The central dual-conditioning idea is clear and practically useful. Recent frames provide motion continuity, while target-view projections from a static 3D memory provide long-range spatial constraints without modifying the DiT backbone.
The static-scene extraction pipeline thoughtfully combines flow inconsistency, backward point tracking, and SAM2 propagation to prevent moving objects from being frozen into the 3D memory.

Results are consistently favorable across scene consistency, camera control, geometric consistency, and perceptual-quality metrics on multiple datasets. The improvements over DFoT in PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and MEt3R are particularly substantial.
The paper includes useful component studies covering dynamic masking, temporal-window size, number of projected views, alternative geometry estimators, long-video generation, and runtime.
The method is modular and can benefit directly from improved reconstruction systems, as illustrated by the DepthAnything v3 experiment.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not compare directly against several closest recent systems, including Gen3C, ReCamMaster, CameraCtrl II, and SPMem. Although code availability is cited, this leaves both novelty and empirical superiority over the strongest related approaches incompletely established.

The claim of supporting arbitrary-length context is stronger than the evidence. There is no controlled scaling experiment over input length, no analysis of how SLAM, masking, point-cloud storage, or retrieval costs grow with length, and only limited evaluation of autoregressive long-horizon generation.

Some comparisons are confounded by different backbones, conditioning modalities, and training regimes. In particular, the strong FVD and VBench gains may partly reflect the CogVideoX-5B base model rather than the proposed spatial prompting. A controlled CogVideoX baseline trained with the same data and compute is needed.

The revisit-view protocol naturally favors a method that directly projects pixels and geometry recovered from the input. Evaluation on genuinely novel trajectories, varying overlap levels, substantial disocclusion, and inaccurate input poses would better establish generalization beyond reconstruction-assisted copying.

Several ablation results are less conclusive than claimed. In Table 6, intermediate masking stages and even the complete pipeline have worse MEt3R than the no-mask variant, despite the statement that every stage is verified. Across Tables 4 and 8, the choice of seven projected views is also not consistently optimal.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the camera-overlap retrieval rule, dynamic threshold, zero-padding and temporal alignment of conditioning tensors, filtering criteria, losses, sampling settings, and baseline adaptation details are underspecified, while code is only promised.

The approach depends heavily on external geometry, flow, tracking, and segmentation models. Failure cases involving poor calibration, stationary foreground objects, large non-rigid motion, reflective surfaces, severe occlusion, or sparse scene coverage are not systematically evaluated.

There is no human evaluation or uncertainty analysis, and the paper does not discuss broader ethical considerations associated with controllable realistic video generation or the provenance and licensing implications of the training data.
